narrative:
The model predicted an 80% chance that you would fail the bar exam on your first attempt. Because the admissions process uses this prediction to assess likely success in law school and beyond, your application was rejected.

The decision was driven primarily by three factors, ranked by importance. Your first-year and third-year class rankings had the strongest influence, followed closely by your LSAT score. All three pushed the prediction strongly toward failure.

Your first-year ranking placed you in the bottom decile of your class, far below the average of sixth decile among accepted students. Similarly, your third-year ranking was also in the bottom decile, compared to an average around the middle of the class for those who were admitted. These unusually low academic standings within your own school signaled to the model a pattern of struggle that strongly increased the estimated risk of failing the bar. Your LSAT score of 19.3 was also well below the average of 37 among accepted applicants, providing another substantial push toward predicting failure.

Your undergraduate GPA of 3.20 was only slightly below the accepted average of 3.23, so it played little role. Your family income, gender, race, and full-time status were not factors in the decision.

To improve your chances, focus on strengthening your academic record and consider retaking the LSAT to raise your score significantly. Targeted bar exam preparation courses or a post-baccalaureate program could also help demonstrate readiness for the next application cycle.
